question: Which physical or observational mechanisms can reduce the complete-band blue/core residual at phase 0.3761495834419293 to 0.3932225607463806?
selection: Post-hoc follow-up of the previously recorded phase audit; not a new detection test.
baseline: Saved PR13 eight-cell atmosphere, native exposure/pixel observation operator, fixed archived GP hyperparameters, common-reference projection and both stride-two pixel interleaves.
parallel_families: Frozen inner/upper source functions and upper opacity; physically linked population changes where available.
Relative layer velocities and positive longitude-dependent source weighting at fixed opacity.
Low-dimensional stellar-line depth, width and shift variability and broad continuum curvature in the stellar frame.
Primary-literature review and saved-state time-scale/illumination plausibility checks.
comparisons: Use the same complete-band maps for target B/C/R and report collateral changes at other supported phases.
Recompute the conditional GP mean when a spectral prediction changes. Keep data, mask and noise hyperparameters fixed.
Separate fixed shared baseline RV/amplitude responses from fits that re-estimate the same two nuisance parameters.
Compare full native-data Q as a descriptive fixed-covariance score; a lower Q is not a Bayes factor or calibrated significance.
Report both pixel interleaves and, where feasible, order/night or held-out controls and numerical refinement.
Identify which processes already exist in the atmosphere; distinguish diagnostic coefficient changes from self-consistent physical solutions.
limitations: The selected interval is short, with substantial empirical time-block uncertainty and no second-night complete blue support.
A successful frozen response identifies a needed spectral direction, not its unique physical cause.
Local microscopic rates are not coupled radiation/population/thermal relaxation eigenvalues.
No new production atmosphere, likelihood, noise calibration or arbitrary phase cut is adopted by this investigation.
